title: The Tango Belt and playing with Black bands in the district
summary: Asked about the Tango Belt, he says he did not play there but visited district joints with his brother, playing with Black bands.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You reminded me of something. You talked about getting hit on the head in the district or something. What was the Tango Belt? I'm always hearing people talk about the Tango Belt. Do you know what that was?
I couldn't tell you with any authenticity because I'm only talking about what I know.
You didn't play in that area.

No, I will say this. The Charlie Rittner, who was the first white man in this town to slap a bass, used to call it slapping a bass, you know. Wilbur Dinkle, who was known as the Albinaud of the South. Albinaud in our day was the leading jazz piano player. You never heard of Albinaud. There was a million Albinauds in the United States.

My brother Paul played the drums and I had the trumpet. And we visited all the joints of the district. We played with the Negro bands. I could buy them a little shell of beer for a nickel apiece and I was always welcome, John, because they liked the way I played. And it didn't hurt me. I listened to them play, they listened to me. They didn't play my way, but nobody threw us out. And he'd slap that bass and my brother would beat hell out the drums and we'd have a hell of a little bit of a time. And I was welcome. That's how I met Mr. Robichill, Professor Robichill. You ever hear of him? Yeah. Left-handed violinist. You didn't know that, eh?
